strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper frames MAD approximation as a constrained optimization problem (Eq. 1) and provides a rigorous, self-contained proof of uniqueness (Appendix A) that grounds the learning objectives.

The core practical appeal — learning distances from action-free, reward-free state trajectories only — is genuinely useful for offline RL, and the framework's robustness to data quality (random exploration, expert data, fragmented/stitch datasets) is convincingly demonstrated, e.g., the AntMaze Medium Explore setting where MadDist learns from purely random data (0.80 success vs. 0.49 for QRL).

Comprehensive and controlled empirical evaluation: a diverse suite of environments with known ground-truth MAD spanning symmetric/asymmetric, discrete/continuous, stochastic/deterministic settings; multiple evaluation metrics (Spearman, Pearson, Ratio CV); ablations over latent dimension, quasimetric choice, and dataset size; plus a downstream planning task (Table 1) that connects representation quality to task performance.
Good reproducibility: full hyperparameter tables for all methods (including baselines), architecture details, dataset construction, hardware, and environment specifications in Appendices D and G.
Honest identification of scope: the conclusion appropriately notes that MAD is a stepping stone and that recovering the stochastic shortest-path distance is left to future work.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. MadDist is a direct extension of Steccanella and Jonsson (2022): the main changes are substituting a quasimetric for a metric, a scale-invariant loss, and an added contrastive term. TDMadDist is standard temporal-difference bootstrapping with a target network. The proposed dsimple quasimetric (Eq. 3) is a convex combination of ReLU coordinate reductions closely related to existing constructions (Pitis et al., 2020; Wang and Isola, 2022).

Evidence for the headline claim that dsimple 'outperforms more elaborate quasimetrics in the existing literature' is thin: the quasimetric ablation (Figures 5 and 6) is conducted only in CliffWalking, a single low-dimensional environment, so the generality of this claim is not established.

Some empirical inconsistencies and high variance undermine the strength of conclusions. Main-text results are said to be means over three random seeds, but appendix figures report five seeds. In Table 1, differences such as AntMaze Medium Explore (0.80 ± 0.21 vs. 0.49 ± 0.23) overlap substantially under the reported standard deviations, and TDMadDist markedly underperforms MadDist in several Stitch environments (e.g., 0.70–0.74), which is not well explained. No statistical significance testing is provided.

Generalization of the evaluation is limited: all environments are navigation-style (grid/maze) with low-dimensional state observations (the 'noisy observations' test adds only two noise dimensions). There is no evidence on image-based or higher-dimensional sensory settings, which limits the claim that this is a general state-representation framework.

The framing of Lo as a proxy for the maximization objective is heuristic; no convergence, consistency, or approximation-error guarantees are given for MadDist/TDMadDist, and the equilibrium argument in Appendix C.3 is informal.

Potential confounds in the downstream planning comparison: the planner uses the true simulator and, for AntMaze, retrieves dataset segments nearest under the learned metric, so Table 1 partially conflates metric quality with dataset retrieval behavior; the effect of this design on baseline comparisons is not analyzed.

Minor presentation issues: inconsistencies in seed counts, duplicated/ambiguous loss notation between MadDist and TDMadDist (e.g., L_c sampling distributions), and discussion in Section 7 that partially mischaracterizes TDMadDist's relative performance.

strengths: The problem of estimating Minimum Action Distance (MAD) from state-only trajectories is well motivated, and the paper clearly positions asymmetric (quasimetric) estimation as an underexplored gap relative to prior symmetric approaches (Steccanella & Jonsson 2022, Hilbert representations, Laplacian methods).

The evaluation suite with ground-truth MAD (NoisyGridWorld, KeyDoorGridWorld, CliffWalking, PointMaze variants, OGBench PointMaze/AntMaze) is a genuine contribution, enabling controlled measurement of representation quality rather than only downstream proxy metrics.

The empirical results are consistent across environments: MadDist achieves near-perfect correlation and strong downstream planning success rates (Table 1), including from undirected 'explore' data and stitched trajectories, and ablations on latent dimension, quasimetric choice, and dataset size are provided.

The theoretical material (uniqueness proof for the constrained formulation, quasimetric properties of d_simple, derivation of the learning objectives) is correct and adds clarity to how the objectives relate to the underlying optimization problem.
Hyperparameter tables, hardware details, and per-environment descriptions are provided, giving reasonable reproducibility information within the text.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: MadDist is essentially Steccanella & Jonsson (2022)'s objective with (i) a scale-invariant loss and (ii) a quasimetric in place of a metric, and TDMadDist is standard TD bootstrapping with a target network. The 'novel quasimetric' d_simple is a trivial convex combination of max and mean ReLU reductions; its claimed superiority over IQE/WideNorm is supported only by ablations in CliffWalking, a single small environment.

Baseline coverage is thin and comparisons are not fully fair. QRL (Wang et al., 2023a) is an online RL method adapted to offline use and, as the authors note, only uses locality constraints, whereas MadDist is supervised with path distances over arbitrary trajectory pairs — the comparison confounds supervision signal with algorithmic contribution. Notably missing: contrastive successor features (Myers et al., 2024), which the paper itself identifies as handling asymmetry, EMAQ, METRA, and other temporal-distance methods.

No theoretical or empirical identifiability analysis of when MAD is recoverable from state trajectories alone. The trajectory upper bounds j−i depend heavily on behavior-policy coverage; claims that the approach is 'agnostic to the data-collection policy' and works with 'datasets of any quality' are asserted but only tested on datasets with broad coverage (random exploration, noisy expert navigate data).

Statistical rigor is marginal: three seeds for the main results (min/max shaded regions), with large variances in Table 1 (e.g., 0.80±0.21, 0.93±0.17), while TDMadDist — one of the two proposed contributions — consistently underperforms both MadDist and sometimes QRL, weakening the overall narrative.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness: Figure 3's caption reports three seeds while appendix figures report five; Table 2 lists hyperparameter ranges ('wr 1, 10', 'dmax 100, 500') without specifying per-environment values, suggesting undisclosed per-task tuning; duplicate/inconsistent citations of Loshchilov & Hutter; 'Glorot et al. (2011)' cited for ReLU.
There is no explicit limitations section, and no code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility and community uptake of the benchmark suite.

The significance beyond small/medium grid and maze domains is untested: no pixel-based observations, no higher-dimensional control beyond AntMaze, and the downstream planner relies on the true simulator, so the reported planning gains partly reflect metric quality in settings where the ground-truth MAD was approximated on a discretized maze graph rather than derived from the true dynamics.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: learning a directed (quasimetric) state distance from reward- and action-free state trajectories, in contrast to prior symmetric approximations of the Minimum Action Distance.

The proposed MadDist and TDMadDist algorithms are technically sound, with a clean derivation (Appendix C) connecting the constrained optimization formulation of the MAD (with a correct uniqueness proof in Appendix A) to tractable learning objectives. The scale-invariant loss is a sensible and well-justified design choice.

The proposed d_simple quasimetric is simple, computationally cheap, and the paper carefully verifies its properties (triangle inequality, positive homogeneity) in Appendix B. The ablations show it outperforms IQE and WideNorm variants.

The introduction of a benchmark suite with known ground-truth MAD values (spanning deterministic/stochastic dynamics, discrete/continuous states, asymmetric transitions, noisy observations) is a genuine community contribution that enables systematic evaluation of MAD approximation methods, which prior work lacked.

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive: correlation metrics, ablations over latent dimension, quasimetric choice, and dataset size, qualitative maze visualizations, and a downstream goal-reaching planning task (Table 1) demonstrating practical utility, including learning from random 'explore' data and stitched short trajectories.
Implementation details, hyperparameters, and compute resources are well documented, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest relative to prior work: the core framework closely follows Steccanella and Jonsson (2022), with the main changes being the use of a quasimetric instead of a symmetric metric and a scale-invariant loss. TDMadDist is a fairly standard TD/EMA-target-network adaptation that empirically underperforms the non-TD variant, weakening the significance of that contribution.

The baseline set is narrow. Only QRL and Hilbert (Park et al., 2024b) are compared, despite the related work section discussing Laplacian methods, time-contrastive successor features (Myers et al., 2024), METRA, and others. Claims of 'significantly outperforming existing state representation methods' (abstract) are not fully supported by the experiments performed.

The downstream planning evaluation is somewhat artificial: the planner uses the true environment simulator to roll out candidate action sequences and, for AntMaze, retrieves trajectory segments from the dataset. This conflates the metric's utility with access to ground-truth dynamics, and the evaluation does not include goal-conditioned RL, even though goal-conditioned RL is a headline motivation in the abstract and introduction.

Experimental rigor is limited: three random seeds in the main experiments (with an inconsistency where appendices claim five seeds), shaded regions reporting min/max rather than confidence intervals, and results restricted to gridworlds and maze navigation. There are no high-dimensional visual observation or realistic robotics experiments, so generalization claims are hard to assess.

Some design choices are under-analyzed: the contrastive loss Lr pushes all random state pairs toward a single hyperparameter d_max, which seems crude and poorly justified in asymmetric environments; the sensitivity to d_max and w_r is not ablated. The TD variant's failure relative to MadDist is acknowledged but not explained or analyzed.

No explicit limitations section is provided in the main text; limitations (e.g., MAD being only a lower bound in stochastic environments, reliance on state coverage, additive noise assumptions) are deferred to brief remarks in the conclusion.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: learning the Minimum Action Distance (MAD) from reward-free, action-free state trajectories is a useful building block for goal-conditioned RL and reward shaping, and the paper correctly identifies that prior symmetric approximations cannot capture the asymmetry of the true MAD in irreversible environments.

Clean theoretical framing: the constrained-optimization characterization of the MAD (Equation 1), the pointwise-maximality result (Theorem 1/2), and the accompanying proof in Appendix A are correct and provide a principled connection between MAD and the LP formulation of all-pairs shortest paths. The reduction of the problem via quasimetric embeddings is clearly derived (Appendix C).

Strong and honest empirical methodology: the benchmark suite spans deterministic/stochastic dynamics, discrete/continuous states, noisy observations, and asymmetric transitions, with ground-truth MAD computed exactly (or via Floyd–Warshall/BFS), enabling controlled, quantitative evaluation rather than only indirect downstream metrics. Multiple complementary metrics (Spearman, Pearson, Ratio CV) with five seeds are used.

The downstream planning evaluation is designed thoughtfully as a controlled diagnostic: a deliberately weak random-shooting planner with the true simulator isolates the quality of the learned distance, avoiding confounds from full RL pipelines. Good ablations cover latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size, network capacity, contrastive weight, and constraint horizon.

Results are convincing within the evaluated scope: MadDist consistently outperforms QRL, PlanDist, PlanDist-Simple, and Hilbert baselines on both distance accuracy (Figures 3, 14–16) and planning success rates (Table 1), including the hard Stitch and Explore (random data) settings, and the ablation comparing PlanDist-Simple to MadDist credibly isolates the contribution of the revised objective beyond the quasimetric alone.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: MadDist is essentially the prior PlanDist method (Steccanella and Jonsson, 2022) with (i) a quasimetric in place of a symmetric metric and (ii) a scale-invariant loss; TDMadDist applies standard TD bootstrapping with a target network. The simple quasimetric of Equation 4 is a minor variation of known ReLU-based constructions. The paper is best viewed as a careful combination and evaluation rather than a fundamentally new method.

No statistical or approximation guarantees for the data-driven relaxation: the theoretical analysis covers only the oracle problem (Equation 1) with known one-step relation R. Once upper-bound constraints from trajectories replace R, there is no analysis of when the learned estimator is consistent (e.g., dependence on behavior-policy coverage, trajectory length distribution, or state coverage). The L_tau target j−i is a biased proxy except on geodesic trajectories, and this bias is not characterized.

Reproducibility concerns: the code-availability statements (in the abstract-level Section 7 and Appendix D) read 'The source code will be publicly released at:' followed by no actual URL. Given that evaluation relies on a bespoke environment suite and subtle implementation choices (e.g., dmax=500, Hc=6, batch structure), this weakens reproducibility at review time.

Scope of empirical claims: results are confined to maze/gridworld-style navigation. There are no pixel-based observations, no integration into full RL pipelines (where the claimed benefits to policy learning and reward shaping are motivated but untested), and the asymmetry benefits are demonstrated mainly in CliffWalking, KeyDoorGridWorld, and the teleport variant.

Some methodological confounds remain in the planning evaluation: for AntMaze, the planner derives candidate actions from dataset trajectory segments selected using the learned distance itself, so success partly depends on dataset segment coverage rather than purely on metric quality; this is acknowledged only partially. Also inconsistent hyperparameters between MadDist (wr=10) and TDMadDist (wr=1) make the head-to-head comparison between the two proposed methods less clean.

Inconsistencies in claims: TDMadDist is proposed as a co-equal contribution but underperforms both MadDist and QRL in most settings, and the discussion of its relative merit is somewhat qualitative; the paper could better delineate when the TD variant is preferable.

strengths: The idea of learning the Minimum Action Distance offline from action- and reward-free state trajectories is well motivated, and the paper positions it clearly against prior work on temporal-distance and quasimetric-based representations.

The characterization of MAD as the unique pointwise-maximal feasible solution of a constrained optimization problem (Theorems 1-2) is correct and gives a clean conceptual grounding, even if elementary.

The controlled evaluation with environments where ground-truth MAD is known (including asymmetric domains like CliffWalking, KeyDoorGridWorld, and teleport mazes) is a genuinely useful contribution and enables direct metric-accuracy assessment (Pearson/Spearman correlation, Ratio CV) that is impossible in standard RL benchmarks.

The ablation studies (latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size, constraint horizon, contrastive weight) are reasonably thorough, and the PlanDist-Simple ablation helpfully isolates that gains come from more than the quasimetric alone.
The downstream planning evaluation is designed thoughtfully as a controlled diagnostic, with a deliberate attempt to isolate representation quality from policy-learning confounds.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. MadDist is essentially PlanDist (Steccanella and Jonsson, 2022) with (i) a quasimetric in place of a symmetric norm and (ii) a rescaled loss; TDMadDist applies standard TD bootstrapping with a target network. The proposed d_simple quasimetric is a trivial convex combination of max and mean of ReLU'd coordinate differences, closely related to existing constructions (Pitis et al. 2020; Wang and Isola 2022). The theoretical result formalizes the well-known LP formulation of all-pairs shortest paths.

Experimental scope is narrow: almost all environments are maze/gridworld navigation tasks. No locomotion tasks beyond maze navigation, no vision-based observations, and no integration into a full goal-conditioned RL pipeline, so claims about downstream RL benefits (goal-conditioned RL, reward shaping) remain untested.

Baseline fairness is questionable. The Hilbert baseline performs dramatically worse than everything else (e.g., 0.01-0.22 success), and QRL - originally an online method - is repurposed for offline trajectory data; the paper's own ablations (Figures 8-9) suggest architecture sensitivity, but hyperparameter tuning effort across methods is not documented, making the 'decisively outperforms all baselines' claims hard to trust.

Internal tension in results: TDMadDist underperforms even QRL on several environments in Table 1 (e.g., 0.39 vs 0.49 on AntMaze Medium Explore; 0.70 vs 0.97 on PointMaze Large Navigate), which undercuts the abstract's blanket claim that 'the proposed approach learns MAD representations more efficiently' and that TD bootstrapping was beneficial.

Reproducibility is weak: the 'Code Availability' and 'source code will be publicly released at' statements are literally empty (no URL), the learning objectives involve many hyperparameters (wr, wc, dmax, Hc, beta) with tuning procedures undescribed, and several key details (how test state pairs are sampled for correlation metrics, how dmax is set per environment) are not specified.

The planning evaluation for AntMaze retrieves action segments from the navigate dataset using the learned distance, which conflates metric quality with dataset-retrieval effects and gives methods trained on navigate-like data a potential advantage; the paper acknowledges but does not analyze this confound.

No discussion of failure modes or limitations of the trajectory-upper-bound approach: the method relies on behavior policies whose trajectories actually connect distant states; in highly stochastic or rarely-crossing environments the upper bounds may be very loose, and this is not analyzed.
Missing comparisons to relevant recent alternatives (e.g., Myers et al. 2024's time-contrastive successor features, METRA) beyond brief textual dismissal.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: learning MAD representations offline from state-only trajectories without actions or rewards, which is practically valuable for goal-conditioned RL and reward shaping.

The formal characterization of MAD as the pointwise-maximal feasible solution of a constrained optimization problem (Theorem 1/2) gives a clean theoretical grounding and transparently connects the learning objectives to the ideal formulation; the derivation from the idealized problem to the tractable losses (Appendix C) is clear and honest about what is being relaxed.

The evaluation is unusually rigorous for this area: environments with known ground-truth MAD spanning deterministic/stochastic dynamics, discrete/continuous states, asymmetric transitions, noisy observations, and stitched/random datasets, evaluated with three complementary metrics (Spearman, Pearson, Ratio CV) over five seeds.

Baselines are appropriate and informative: the PlanDist-Simple variant cleverly isolates the contribution of the quasimetric from the objective redesign, and the analysis of MadDist vs. TDMadDist vs. Hilbert disentangles representation parametrization from TD learning.

Extensive ablations (latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size, network size, contrastive weight, constraint horizon) support robustness claims, and the downstream planning experiment is framed as a controlled diagnostic (using a simple planner with the true simulator), which is a defensible way to attribute performance to representation quality rather than planner sophistication.
Implementation details are thorough (hyperparameter tables for all methods, compute resources, evaluation protocol), suggesting good reproducibility once code is released.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: MadDist is essentially PlanDist (Steccanella & Jonsson, 2022) with three modifications (quasimetric distance, scale-invariant loss, contrastive term); TDMadDist is standard TD bootstrapping with a target network; and d_simple is a straightforward max/mean ReLU difference quasimetric closely related to existing constructions (Wide Norm, IQE). Theorem 1 largely restates the known equivalence between the constrained problem and all-pairs shortest paths.

The paper claims the benchmark suite as a contribution, but several environments are modest grid worlds or minor extensions of existing benchmarks (D4RL/OGBench mazes), and the ground-truth MAD for continuous mazes is only an approximation via grid discretization.

Evidence for the central asymmetry claim could be stronger: asymmetric structure is present only in a subset of environments (KeyDoor, CliffWalking, Teleport), and the headline accuracy figures (Fig. 3) are dominated by symmetric maze tasks; a direct quantification of where quasimetrics beat symmetric metrics on asymmetric environments would better support the framing.

TDMadDist, one of the two proposed algorithms, consistently underperforms MadDist and even QRL in several environments (e.g., AntMaze Medium Explore: 0.39 vs 0.80), and the paper does not clearly articulate when or why the TD variant should be preferred, weakening the value of the second contribution.

No explicit limitations section; caveats are deferred to future work (e.g., MAD ignores stochasticity since it depends only on transition support, and trajectory-derived upper bounds can only bound the support from observed data). This deserves clearer acknowledgment as a limitation of what the method can recover.

Statistical reporting is limited to mean ± standard deviation over five seeds without significance testing; some comparisons (e.g., MadDist vs. TDMadDist or vs. PlanDist-Simple in Table 1) have overlapping intervals and high variance, making some conclusions less certain than stated.
Code availability is stated as 'will be publicly released at:' with no link, so reproducibility cannot be verified at review time.

The downstream planning evaluation uses the true simulator and, for AntMaze, retrieves trajectory segments from the navigate dataset, which introduces dataset access asymmetries across methods that are only partially discussed.
